plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single vector-field plot inside a square frame. The horizontal axis is labeled "x (m)" with ticks from -2 to 4, the vertical axis "y (m)" with ticks from -2 to 2. The field appears as a regular grid of dark blue arrows whose lengths vary sharply with position, shrinking toward the edges of the frame until they read as bare dots. Two centers of activity stand out, both on the line y = 0. Around the origin the arrows are long and point radially outward in every direction. Around the point at x = 2, y = 0 they are just as long but point radially inward, converging on that spot. Between and around the pair they take intermediate directions, turning from the outward pattern on the left into the inward pattern on the right and shortening with distance from either center. No source objects or charge symbols are drawn; the arrows alone stand for the field. Packing direction and magnitude into hundreds of separate arrows is what makes the pattern dense and awkward to follow. The plot motivates replacing the grid with continuous field lines that carry the same information without the clutter.

interactionPlan.concept: The electric field of a dipole is a vector at every point — the sum of an outward field from the positive charge and an inward field from the negative charge — and a grid of arrows and a set of continuous field lines are two representations of that same one field.
elements: Square plot frame with thin black border
Horizontal axis labeled 'x (m)' with ticks and numerals at -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
Vertical axis labeled 'y (m)' with ticks and numerals at -2, -1, 0, 1, 2
Regular square grid of dark navy-blue arrows filling the whole frame, arrow length proportional to local field magnitude (capped near the singularities)
Source point at (0, 0): arrows radiate outward in all directions, longest nearby (positive charge location, unmarked in the original)
Sink point at (2, 0): arrows converge inward from all directions (negative charge location, unmarked in the original)
Transition region between x = 0 and x = 2 where arrows turn from outward to inward and point predominantly in the +x direction along the axis
Outer regions where arrows shrink to near-invisible dots, showing 1/r^2 falloff
Optional overlay: continuous field-line curves leaving (0,0) and terminating on (2,0), with small arrowheads along each curve indicating direction
Optional hover overlay: enlarged sampled arrow, two thinner component arrows (red from +q, blue toward -q) drawn tail-to-tail at the sampled point, dashed parallelogram closing to the resultant
Hover readout box: coordinates (x, y) and |E| in arbitrary units with the two contributing magnitudes
Small legend: '+q at (0,0)', '-q at (2,0)', 'arrow length ∝ |E|'

interactions.teaches: Arrows and field lines carry the same directional information; field lines trade per-point magnitude for a readable global picture of flow from positive to negative charge.
interactions.label: Representation

interactions.teaches: Each drawn arrow is not a primitive object but the vector sum of one field pointing away from +q and one pointing toward -q, evaluated at that single point.
Clutter is a property of the sampling, not of the field: the dipole pattern is identical whether you draw 100 arrows or 2500.
interactions.label: Grid samples per side

demo_steps.title: The raw vector grid
demo_steps.narration: Hundreds of arrows on a square grid show the field everywhere at once. Two hot spots sit on y = 0: arrows fly outward from (0,0) and pile inward at (2,0), while everything far away fades to dots.

demo_steps.title: Thin the sampling
demo_steps.narration: Drop to a coarse grid. The arrows are fewer and easier to read, yet the outward-then-inward dipole pattern is unchanged — the clutter came from how densely we sampled, not from the field itself.

demo_steps.title: One point, two contributions
demo_steps.narration: Hover any arrow. Two component arrows appear — one pointing away from the positive charge at (0,0), one pointing toward the negative charge at (2,0) — and their sum is exactly the arrow that was already drawn there.

demo_steps.title: Connect the arrows into lines
demo_steps.narration: Now link arrows tip-to-tail into continuous curves. Every line starts on the positive charge and ends on the negative charge, and the crowding of lines near the charges replaces arrow length as the magnitude cue.

demo_steps.title: Same field, two pictures
demo_steps.narration: With both overlaid, every arrow lies tangent to a field line. The two representations are the same information; field lines simply say it with far less ink.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Every arrow in the plot is just the vector sum of 'away from +q' and 'toward -q' at that spot — so the field lines you draw later aren't new physics, they're the same vectors joined tangentially and drawn without the clutter.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Square white plot area with a thin black border, generous white margin. Bold axis labels 'x (m)' below and rotated 'y (m)' at left; x ticks -2..4, y ticks -2..2, equal aspect ratio. Fill the frame with a uniform grid of dark navy (#1F3864 / midnight blue) arrows with small solid arrowheads; scale length by |E| with a cap so near-charge arrows stay ~0.35 grid units, and let far-field arrows shrink to single pixels/dots. Field is E = k[(r - r0)/|r - r0|^3 - (r - r1)/|r - r1|^3] with r0 = (0,0), r1 = (2,0). Radial outward starburst at the origin, radial inward convergence at (2,0), arrows along the segment between them pointing in +x, and arrows above/below the pair sweeping in arcs from left source to right sink. Field-line view: ~14 smooth curves emerging evenly around (0,0) and terminating evenly around (2,0), same navy color, thinner strokes, small arrowheads placed periodically along each curve; the straight line along the x-axis between the charges is one of them. Hover overlay: highlight the nearest grid arrow in orange, draw two translucent component arrows (warm red from +q, cool blue toward -q) tail-to-tail from the hovered point with a dashed parallelogram closing to the resultant, plus a small light readout card showing (x, y), |E+|, |E-|, and |E_total| in arbitrary units. Density slider simply re-samples the same analytic field; never redraw or move the charges. No charge glyphs in the default view — optionally show faint '+' and '−' markers only when the hover or field-line view is active.

authoredContext:
This diagram is correct, but it becomes less useful as the source charge distribution becomes more complicated. For example, consider the vector field diagram of a dipole (the figure).

The vector field of a dipole. Even with just two identical charges, the vector field diagram becomes difficult to understand.

A vector plot of the electric field due to two sources. The sources are not shown. The field is represented by arrows in an x y graph. Both x and y are in meters and both scales are from -2 meters to 4 meters. Near the origin, the arrows are long and point away from it. Near the point at coordinates 2, 0 the arrows are long and point toward the point. The arrows get smaller as we move farther from those two location and point in intermediate directions.

There is a more useful way to present the same information. Rather than drawing a large number of increasingly smaller vector arrows, we instead connect all of them together, forming continuous lines and curves, as shown in the figure.

discrepancies: Axis titles are duplicated and overlap: the screenshot shows 'x (m)' drawn twice on top of itself ('xx((mm))') and the same for the rotated 'y (m)', because drawAxes() appends titles to gLabels which is never cleared between layout() calls — the source has single clean bold italic axis titles.

Arrow lengths near the charges are longer and more crowded than in the source; neighbouring arrows overlap into a starburst/smear around (0,0) and (2,0) instead of the source's short, clearly separated arrows with visible whitespace.

The immediate neighbourhood of the +q charge at (0,0) reads as a pale gap in the generated figure, whereas the source shows a distinct dense radial hedgehog of outward arrows there of comparable visual weight to the −q sink.

Far-field samples in the source degrade to tiny dots on a regular lattice; in the generated figure they render as short dashes/strokes with visible direction, changing the 'fading to dots' texture of the background.

The generated arrow field appears to include a slightly different sampling offset so the grid rows/columns no longer align symmetrically about y = 0 the way the source lattice does (a row of near-horizontal strokes sits exactly on y = 0 rather than straddling it).
evaluation.notes: Physically correct dipole vector grid with an excellent interaction set (representation toggle, density slider, hover superposition decomposition, 5-step demo), but the duplicated, mutually overlapping x- and y-axis titles make the labelling look broken and arrow lengths near the charges are longer/more crowded than the source.
action_items: Clear gLabels (or a dedicated axis-title group) at the start of drawAxes() so the 'x (m)' and 'y (m)' titles are not re-appended on every layout/resize, eliminating the overlapping doubled text.

Reduce Lmax (e.g. cap arrow length near ~0.9× grid spacing and lower the magnitude saturation) so arrows near (0,0) and (2,0) do not overlap neighbours, matching the source's shorter, well-separated arrows.
Render very weak far-field samples as small dots (tiny filled circles) rather than short directional dashes, to reproduce the source's dotted background texture.
Balance the two poles visually: ensure the outward arrows around +q at (0,0) are as dense and prominent as the inward arrows at −q, avoiding the pale gap currently visible at the origin.

feedback.rationale: Concept and interaction plan are sound (concept 5, interactivity 5) and all action items are concrete implementation fixes—clearing the label group to stop duplicated axis titles, capping arrow length, and rendering far-field samples as dots.

Arrow heads/shafts in the generated figure are thinner and slightly more uniform in width; the source uses a slightly heavier navy stroke with more visible triangular heads at larger sizes.
